introduction-the-entropy-of-infrastructu.core: Infrastructure naturally drifts from code: emergency console fixes, other automation, provider defaults changing, and resources deleted or modified by people who don't know they're Terraform-managed. Detecting drift is only half the job; each drift needs a decision (revert to code, or adopt into code) and a workflow that makes that decision quickly and safely.

first_principles.problem: Nightly drift reports list 140 differences and everyone ignores them.

analogy.title: A desk that gets messier every week
analogy.story: Noticing the mess doesn't tidy it; you need a habit of putting things back or deciding where they now belong.
analogy.breaks: Desks don't get hacked; drifted security groups do.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Noise removed; real issues acted on.

check.q: Why can a drift report become useless?
check.a: Without classification and ownership, benign noise drowns real issues and people stop reading it.

remediation-workflows-manual-vs-automate.core: Manual remediation treats drift as an alert: a scheduled plan detects it, opens a ticket or PR, and a human decides. That is safe during incidents but slow. Automated remediation re-applies code on detection, which is fast and consistent but can revert a legitimate emergency fix mid-incident. Most teams combine them: auto-revert high-risk security drift, human review for the rest.

first_principles.problem: An auto-apply drift job reverts an on-call engineer's emergency capacity increase during an outage.

analogy.title: A smoke alarm vs a sprinkler system
analogy.story: Alarms let a human judge; sprinklers act instantly but soak everything, including false alarms.
analogy.breaks: Sprinklers don't know about incidents; your automation must.

check.q: What guard should automated drift remediation have?
check.a: Awareness of active incidents or change freezes so it doesn't revert emergency fixes.

the-import-path-adopting-legitimate-chan.core: When reality is right and code is wrong (a valid hotfix, or a resource created outside Terraform), adopt it rather than revert it. Update the code to match the changed attribute (the plan then shows no change), or for new unmanaged resources add an import block and config. Verify with a zero-diff plan, and merge through a normal PR so the change is reviewed and recorded.

first_principles.problem: A hotfix raised an RDS max_connections parameter; the next apply silently reverts it and causes another outage.
truths: Code must catch up to reality.

analogy.title: Updating the map after a new road is built
analogy.story: The road is real and useful; you redraw the map rather than bulldoze the road.
analogy.breaks: Maps can lag; IaC should catch up within days.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Plan shows no changes; reality and code agree.

check.a: Updates state to match reality without changing infrastructure, useful when accepting drift into state before updating code.

event-driven-iac-the-immune-system.core: Polling for drift every 24 hours leaves long windows of exposure. Event-driven IaC reacts to changes as they happen: CloudTrail API events flow through EventBridge to rules that detect writes to managed resources, for example by checking a managed-by tag or a non-pipeline principal. These trigger a targeted plan, an alert, or an immediate fix, like an immune system responding to infection.

first_principles.problem: A security group opened via the console stays open for 23 hours until the nightly drift job.

analogy.title: White blood cells vs annual check-ups
analogy.story: The body responds to infection in minutes; it doesn't wait for next year's check-up.
analogy.breaks: Immune systems can overreact; tune rules to avoid auto-reverting legit changes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Any non-CI SG ingress change triggers a revert pipeline within minutes.

check.q: How can you tell an out-of-band change from a pipeline change in CloudTrail?
check.a: By the principal: changes not made by the CI/Terraform role (userIdentity) are out-of-band.

choosing-a-remediation-strategy-a-decisi.core: Segment resources by risk and operational reality instead of one policy for all. Security-critical config (IAM, security groups, public access) gets event-driven auto-revert. Stateful and incident-touched resources (databases, capacity) get alert plus human decision. Externally managed fields (ASG desired count, Lambda versions deployed by CI) get ignore_changes. Low-risk drift gets a weekly batch review.

first_principles.problem: A single 'auto-revert everything' policy keeps breaking autoscaling and incident response.

analogy.title: Hospital triage
analogy.story: Critical patients get immediate action, others are scheduled, and some just need monitoring.
analogy.breaks: Triage nurses judge each case; your rules must be written in advance.

check.q: When is ignore_changes the right remediation choice?
check.a: When another system legitimately owns that attribute, such as autoscaling owning desired capacity.
